<strong>El recuento.</strong> Siete piez: The count. Seven pieces: sea, n12, =, 3, +, 4, ;. The two spaces appear nowhere.
<strong>Las tres primeras letras.</stron: The first three letters. Letters are read while there are any: out comes sea, and since it is in the list of seven, it is a palabra. The space is thrown away.
<strong>Los números y el resto.</strong>: The numbers and the rest. 3 is a num: digits are read until the + appears, which is not a digit, so it closes the piece without consuming it. Then + (op), 4 (num) and ; (op).
<strong>Los símbolos.</strong> <code>=</: The symbols. = is an op. The splitter looks to see whether with the next character it forms one of the double ones, ==, <=, >=, !=, and since it does not, it leaves it as a single one.
<strong>Un nombre con cifras dentro.</st: A name with digits inside. It starts with a letter, so letters and digits are read: out comes n12, which is not in the list, so it is a nombre. Notice that a name can carry digits, but not start with one.

El lenguaje que se construye en esta seg: The language built in this second half is called Pizca, Spanish for “a pinch”, which is what it amounts to: seven words, four operations and six comparisons. That is enough to write any calculation, and that so little should be enough is itself part of what has to be learnt.
El primer compilador, el A-0 de <strong>: The first compiler, Grace Hopper's A-0 (1952), did not split much: it worked by joining pieces of already written code. The idea of separating splitting from the rest arrived with FORTRAN and became a formal technique in the sixties, when it was proved that the tokens of any reasonable language can be described with regular expressions and recognised with a finite automaton. Out of that came lex, a 1975 program you give the list of expressions and which hands back the splitter, written. That it could be automated is what turned writing a compiler into something that fits in a course.

The splitter does not need to understand anything. It goes character by character with a state and one rule per state, which is exactly the definition of an automaton you saw in [[lg-algoritmos|algorithms]]:

The [[maq-ensamblador|assembler]] was already a translator, but one so modest it hardly shows: one line, one instruction. A programming language is another matter.

Eso de «cierra la pieza sin consumir el: That business of “closing the piece without consuming the character” is the only subtlety in the matter, and it has a name: look without eating. The splitter needs to see the next character to know that the number has ended, but it cannot keep it, because it is the start of the next piece. An analyser that eats that character loses pieces along the way, and it is the classic mistake of whoever writes their first splitter.
Esto no es solo cosa de compiladores. Ca: This is not only a compiler matter. Every time a program reads a configuration file, a CSV spreadsheet, a hand-written date or a search query, the first thing it does is this very thing. And when something goes wrong reading data, the fault is almost always here: in a separator that appeared inside a value, in a number with a comma where a point was expected, in an extra space. Half of practical computing is splitting other people's text carefully.
Fíjate en lo que <strong>desaparece</str: Notice what disappears when splitting: the spaces, the line breaks and the comments. They are not pieces, they are separators; once the cut is made they are not needed again. That is why it makes no difference whether the program is written cramped or with pretty indentation: for the pieces it is the same.
Hay que <strong>mirar sin comer</strong>: You have to look without eating: the character that closes a piece is the first of the next.
Hay que leer letras hasta que se acaben: Letters have to be read until they run out and then the list consulted. Otherwise a variable called seamos would break the splitter.
La diferencia se ve con un ejemplo. Esto: The difference shows with an example. This is a single line:

Los espacios no cuentan. Un número enter: Spaces do not count. A whole number is a single piece even if it has several digits, and each separate symbol, the semicolon included, is one.
Spaces are separators: they are thrown away. The two lines give exactly the same pieces.
Los espacios, los saltos de línea y los: Spaces, line breaks and comments disappear: they are separators, not pieces.

Por dentro es un <strong>autómata</stron: Inside it is an automaton: a state and one rule per state, character by character.

Se coge siempre la pieza más larga posib: The longest possible piece is always taken, and whether something is a word of the language is decided only after reading it whole.
Everything up to the end of the line is thrown away. A comment never becomes a piece.
Si está <em>parado</em> y llega un espac: If it is idle and a space arrives, it throws it away and stays idle.
Si está leyendo número y llega otra cifr: If it is reading a number and another digit arrives, it adds it and stays as it is; if anything else arrives, it closes the piece and goes back to idle without consuming that character.
Si está parado y llega una cifra, pasa a: If it is idle and a digit arrives, it moves to reading a number.
Siete piezas de una línea de catorce car: Seven pieces from a line of fourteen characters. And from here on, the rest of the translator never looks at the text again: it works only with the list.
Sigue en el mismo estado, añadiendo cifr: It stays in the same state, adding digits, until something that is not one appears.
Trocea las dos a mano y compara las list: Split the two by hand and compare the lists. Remember which things never become pieces.
Trocear es lo primero que hace cualquier: Splitting is the first thing any translator does, and from then on the original text is never looked at again.
Un <strong>token</strong> es un trozo de: A token is a piece of text with a name: number, name, word of the language or symbol.
Un nombre admite cifras a partir del seg: A name admits digits from the second character on: n12 is a single name. The automaton stays in the same state and adds it.
Un número se acaba en cuanto llega algo: A number ends as soon as something arrives that is not a digit. It closes the piece and goes back to idle without consuming the letter, which will be the start of the next one.
Un programa llega como una ristra de car: A program arrives as a string of characters: m, u, e, s… Nobody can work like that. The first thing is to group the characters into named pieces, which are called tokens. Each says what it is and what text formed it:
Un salto de línea es un separador como c: A line break is a separator like any other. The pieces are the same; the only thing that changes is the line number noted on them.

¿Y cómo distingue <code>sea</code> —que: And how does it tell sea, which is a word of the language, from seat, which would be an ordinary name? It does not tell them apart while reading: it reads letters until they run out and only then looks to see whether what it read is in the list of seven. Trying to decide sooner leads to considerable trouble, and to a program with a variable called seamos failing to compile.
